stances.claim: The standard of fairness in creditor-debtor relationships is that creditors should not recover more than entitled and debtors should not pay more than they justly owe, regardless of what their written agreements provide -- a principle warranting four legislative-regulatory reforms.
stances.rhetorical_move: standard-of-fairness foundational framing for Divina's four proposals

stances.claim: First, the Central Bank should periodically (at least annually) set a range of acceptable interest rates -- because the SC's inconsistent jurisprudence on unconscionable rates (72% struck down 2001, 7%/month upheld 2002, 24%/year struck down 2007, 3%/month struck down to 24%/year 2009) leaves uncertainty on compounded and penalty rates, even after the BSP's July 2013 lowering of the legal rate from 12% to 6%.

Second, creditors should not be allowed to hide behind dragnet clauses to conceal the true amount of secured loans -- though the SC has upheld their validity, they are unfair because debtors may forget them on future loans, future lenders are deprived of full creditworthiness disclosure, and the government is deprived of proper DST and mortgage-registration fees.

Third, for banking-institution mortgagees, the minimum bid at foreclosure sales should equal at least the appraised value -- because the bank-as-bidder can pay a small bid price, own the property, and still collect the deficiency on the outstanding loan, leaving the poor mortgagor liable for the gap.

Fourth, the SC should accredit a list of trustworthy, competent, credible, and readily-available rehabilitation receivers -- courts currently have very little choice on whom to appoint to assist bankrupt corporations because no such accredited list exists.
Divina's closing FLP-aligned thesis: creditor-debtor relationships of fairness and equity lead to efficient and responsible credit use, which in turn promotes economic development and prosperity.

notable_anecdotes: The four-Solangon-Silvestre-Bacolor-Macalinao SC jurisprudence inconsistency catalog (72%/year struck, 7%/month upheld, 24%/year struck, 3%/month struck) -- the most concentrated CJP case-citation on interest-rate doctrine in the corpus, used to argue regulatory clarification beats case-by-case jurisprudence.

The dragnet-clause threefold-unfairness taxonomy (debtor-forgetfulness + future-lender-disclosure-deprivation + DST/registration-fee underdeclaration) -- concise three-element critique of a doctrine the SC has upheld, recommending legislative override.

The banking-mortgage deficiency-after-redemption injustice -- bank pays small bid, owns property, still collects on the balance -- a structural critique of a frequent banking-law trap for poor mortgagors.

The state's-witness-vs-state-witness grammar postscript -- Panganiban's own original 'state witness' (legal) corrected by the eagle-eyed Inquirer opinion editor to 'state's witness' (grammatical) -- a charming epistolary postscript on legal-vs-grammatical usage with the punch line 'readers can choose between being legal and being grammatical.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports on Dean Nilo T. Divina's well-attended UST Faculty of Civil Law public lecture (Divina holds one of the ten Chief Justice Panganiban Professorial Chairs on Liberty and Prosperity and is president of the Philippine Association of Law Schools), with Dean Danilo L. Concepcion of UP and other UST officials in the audience. The lecture's central question: how to satisfy an unpaid creditor without being unfair to a distressed debtor. Divina's standard of fairness -- creditors should not recover more than entitled, debtors should not pay more than they justly owe, regardless of what their written agreements provide -- anchors four proposals. First, the Central Bank should periodically (at least annually) set a range of acceptable interest rates, because the 1982 suspension of the Usury Law left contracting parties free to stipulate any rate, the SC's case-by-case jurisprudence on unconscionable rates is inconsistent (Solangon v. Salazar 2001 struck 72%/year down to 12%, Silvestre v. Ramos 2002 upheld 7%/month, Bacolor v. Banco Filipino 2007 struck 24%/year, Macalinao v. BPI 2009 struck a credit-card 3%/month rate down to 24%/year), and uncertainty on compounded and penalty rates persists even after the BSP's July 1 2013 reduction of the legal rate from 12% to 6%. Second, creditors should not be allowed to hide behind dragnet clauses to conceal the true amount of secured loans -- the SC has upheld their validity, but Divina identifies threefold unfairness: debtors may forget them on future loans, future lenders are deprived of full creditworthiness disclosure, and the government is deprived of proper documentary stamp taxes and mortgage-registration fees. Third, for banking-institution mortgagees, the minimum bid at foreclosure sales should equal at least the appraised value of the property, because a bank-bidder can win with a small bid, own the property, and still collect the deficiency on the outstanding loan, leaving the poor mortgagor liable for the gap. Fourth, the SC should accredit a list of trustworthy, competent, credible, and readily-available rehabilitation receivers, because courts currently have very little choice on whom to appoint for bankrupt corporations. Divina's closing thesis aligns with the FLP: creditor-debtor relationships characterized by fairness and equity lead to efficient and responsible credit use, which in turn promotes economic development and prosperity. Panganiban appends a light grammar postscript on his March 23 2014 column's repeated use of 'state's witness' (the eagle-eyed Inquirer opinion editor's grammatical correction) instead of 'state witness' (the legal term per the Rules of Court), conceding the grammatical correctness while noting that readers can choose between being legal and being grammatical.
